overview: This file traces the acquisition, shipment, inspection, pricing, and eventual compensation dispute surrounding roughly 15,000–17,000 metric tons of lead exported from occupied Japan to the United States after World War II. Early papers connect the shipment to an acute American lead shortage affecting ammunition production, while later British Embassy correspondence argues that ingots bearing Burmese markings were British-owned material looted by Japan and should be returned or properly compensated. The file includes diplomatic correspondence, contracts and amendments, inspection procedures, shipping and accounting schedules, an invoice, title-transfer instruments, and a warranty, documenting how SCAP, the U.S. Commercial Company, the Reconstruction Finance Corporation’s Office of Metals Reserve, and British authorities attempted to reconcile commodity procurement with restitution policy.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on procuring surplus Japanese lead
subfiles.from: C. A. Wendel, IR
subfiles.to: Mr. Kennedy, IR
subfiles.about: Reports an interagency discussion about importing the first 15,000 tons of lead declared surplus in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wendel reports MacArthur releasing 15,000 of 57,000 tons of Japanese lead, pending British agreement and price talks.

subfiles.title: Remington letter on lead quotas and threatened curtailment
subfiles.from: D. F. Carpenter, Remington Arms Company
subfiles.to: Willard L. Thorp, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests help obtaining more lead after the Civilian Production Administration imposed an inadequate ammunition-industry quota.
subfiles.summary: Remington warns its lead quota is too small to avoid shutdowns, framing ammunition output as a defense priority needing a formal appeal.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Remington lead-quota letter
subfiles.from: D. F. Carpenter, Remington Arms Company
subfiles.to: Willard L. Thorp, Department of State
subfiles.about: Duplicates Remington’s request for assistance in augmenting lead supplies.
subfiles.summary: This second copy repeats the company’s account of its 4,410-ton allocation, threatened layoffs, use of low-antimony lead to supplement difficult high-antimony scrap inventories, and planned summer shutdowns. The OCR date of 1940 on page 5 is an error; the duplicate is dated June 21, 1946.

subfiles.title: Thorp reply to Carpenter on the lead shortage
subfiles.from: Willard L. Thorp, Department of State
subfiles.to: D. F. Carpenter, Remington Arms Company
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Remington’s concerns and states that the lead-supply problem is under consideration.
subfiles.summary: Thorp acknowledges Carpenter's complaint on the lead shortage, promising further word after review.

subfiles.title: Whitman request to record markings on Japanese lead
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Department of State
subfiles.to: Jesse C. Johnson, Office of Metals Reserve
subfiles.about: Requests documentation of markings on imported Japanese lead so that looted material can be identified.
subfiles.summary: Whitman asks Metals Reserve to record markings on Japanese lead that may include material looted from Southeast Asia.

subfiles.title: British Embassy warning concerning marked lead
subfiles.from: J. A. Smart, British Embassy
subfiles.to: Marion Worthing, Civilian Production Administration
subfiles.about: Warns that lead bearing specified Burmese markings is British-owned material looted by Japan.
subfiles.summary: Britain warns some Japanese lead bound for the US bears British markings, asking to be notified before shipment.

subfiles.title: Smart letter pressing for return of Burmese lead
subfiles.from: J. A. E. Smart, British Embassy
subfiles.to: Marion Worthing, Civilian Production Administration
subfiles.about: Transmits the British Ministry of Supply’s case that marked lead in Japan was prewar British property and should be shipped to the United Kingdom.
subfiles.summary: Smart says Japan recast pre-invasion Burmese lead rather than mining new stock, so Britain considers marked lead looted property outside Anglo-American allocation.

subfiles.title: British request to reconsider the Japanese lead allocation
subfiles.from: J. A. E. Smart, British Embassy
subfiles.to: Marion Worthing, Civilian Production Administration
subfiles.about: Reopens Britain’s claim to the British-owned portion of 15,000 tons of Japanese lead already shipped to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Britain argues the US got more Japanese lead than Britain got German lead, asking for reconsideration once markings are confirmed.

subfiles.title: Whitman request for a consolidated markings report
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Department of State
subfiles.to: Jesse C. Johnson, Reconstruction Finance Corporation
subfiles.about: Requests a report of the marks and tonnages found on imported Japanese lead and tin.
subfiles.summary: Whitman asks for a consolidated report on markings and tonnage of Japanese tin and lead received by a given date.

subfiles.title: Martin request to record markings on Japanese tin
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Department of State
subfiles.to: Jesse C. Johnson, Office of Metals Reserve
subfiles.about: Requests preservation of identifying marks on 4,000 tons of Japanese tin so its possible Southeast Asian origin can be determined.
subfiles.summary: Martin reports approval to import Japanese tin for assay, asking Metals Reserve to document markings given looting suspicions.

subfiles.title: McKinnon letter on settlement for Burmese-marked lead
subfiles.from: W. F. McKinnon, Office of Metals Reserve
subfiles.to: R. Burr Smith, attention Roger Williams, Department of State
subfiles.about: Supplies contract, price, title-transfer, and accounting information for determining compensation owed Britain for looted Burmese lead.
subfiles.summary: McKinnon details a 17,000-ton US purchase of Japanese lead including Burmese-marked stock, covering pricing, titles, and freight terms.

subfiles.title: Burma lead proceeds, expenses, and vessel schedule
subfiles.from: Office of Metals Reserve
subfiles.to: Department of State
subfiles.about: Provides financial and shipment-level accounting for Burmese-marked lead imported from Japan.
subfiles.summary: The schedules show sales proceeds and claims totaling $1,590,079, expenses of $287,767.15, and net proceeds of $1,302,311.85. A vessel table distributes 18,688,993 pounds among the Mount Rogers, Vanderbilt Victory, Aberdeen Victory, and San Mateo Victory and classifies the metal as corroding, common, or off-grade.

subfiles.title: Hobson letter establishing inspection procedures
subfiles.from: A. T. Hobson
subfiles.to: D. C. Schieck, U.S. Commercial Company
subfiles.about: Proposes standardized inspection, lotting, weighing, and cost-allocation procedures for Japanese tin, lead, and antimony.
subfiles.summary: Hobson sets inspection procedures for Japanese lead and tin shipments, including lot sizes, assays, and special handling for already-sold British-marked lead.

subfiles.title: Levinson proposal for settling off-grade lead lots
subfiles.from: Morris Levinson, Office of Metals Reserve
subfiles.to: U.S. Commercial Company, attention DeWitt C. Schieck
subfiles.about: Proposes payment terms for three Mount Rogers lots containing substandard lead but appreciable tin.
subfiles.summary: Levinson proposes a settlement price for off-grade lead-tin lots based on their actual metal content under existing contracts.

subfiles.title: Johnson amendment increasing the refined-lead price
subfiles.from: Jesse C. Johnson, Office of Metals Reserve
subfiles.to: U.S. Commercial Company, attention DeWitt C. Schieck
subfiles.about: Amends contract P-5151 to pay 8.5 cents per pound for Japanese lead meeting the common-grade specification.
subfiles.summary: Johnson revises the price for high-purity Japanese refined lead to 8.5 cents a pound, with a penalty for lower purity.

subfiles.title: RFC letter revising terms for exports from Japan
subfiles.from: Reconstruction Finance Corporation
subfiles.to: Robert P. Patterson, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Sets revised legal and commercial terms governing merchandise transferred from occupied Japan to the U.S. Commercial Company.
subfiles.summary: RFC letter sets terms for Japanese exports: Japan must vest and transfer clear title to USCC, which can store, sell, and deduct costs plus a 3% fee.

subfiles.title: Invoice for 1,500 metric tons of ESS lead
subfiles.from: Kansai Trade Office of the Trade Board
subfiles.to: U.S. Commercial Company
subfiles.about: Invoices 29,126 ESS lead ingots for shipment from Kobe to New York.
subfiles.summary: Invoice records 1,500 tons of marked lead ingots shipped from Kobe to New York for the US Commercial Company.

subfiles.title: Transfer of title for ESS lead ingots
subfiles.from: Kansai Trade Office of the Trade Board
subfiles.to: U.S. Commercial Company
subfiles.about: Transfers ownership of 29,126 ESS lead ingots to the U.S. Commercial Company for disposal under War Department direction.
subfiles.summary: Instrument transfers title of marked lead ingots to USCC for disposal, confirmed by a SCAP endorsement.

subfiles.title: Warranty of clear title to the invoiced lead
subfiles.from: Kansai Trade Office of the Trade Board
subfiles.to: SCAP, the U.S. War Department, the U.S. Commercial Company, and subsequent recipients
subfiles.about: Guarantees clear title to the lead covered by the attached bill of sale and promises to hold all later parties harmless.
subfiles.summary: Warranty certifies clear title to lead later claimed as British loot, despite the categorical ownership statement.

subfiles.title: Wilson letter on the valuation of Burmese lead
subfiles.from: C. B. Wilson, British Embassy
subfiles.to: R. Burr Smith, Department of State
subfiles.about: Challenges the proposed basis for compensating Britain for Burmese lead shipped from Japan to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Wilson relays a British-US dispute over valuing Burmese lead, asking about remaining stockpiles and how much was looted.

subfiles.title: Smith reply concerning stockpiled Burmese lead
subfiles.from: R. Burr Smith, Department of State
subfiles.to: C. B. Wilson, British Embassy
subfiles.about: Confirms that approximately 1,600 tons remained outside consumption and states the expected basis of SCAP compensation.
subfiles.summary: Smith confirms 1,600 tons of Burmese lead was stockpiled, with SCAP to determine how much Japan looted for British compensation.

interest: Shows how looted lead and tin moved from Japanese custody through SCAP sale to the US, amid British restitution claims.
